summary: Defines CMS Advanced Electronic Signatures, a signature format that can stay valid for a long time, including evidence of validity even if a party later tries to deny it. It extends the Cryptographic Message Syntax. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A signature on paper fades, but a digital signature can also stop proving anything, because the certificate it relied on expires or the algorithm behind it weakens. CAdES adds the missing evidence step by step, so that a signature can still be shown to be genuine years after it was made, and cannot be denied by the person who made it.

how do long term electronic signatures stay valid
subtitle: A signature format built on CMS that can still be proven valid years later, even if someone denies having signed.

tldr.problem: A digital signature depends on certificates, revocation data and algorithms that expire, get revoked or weaken over time, so a signature can become hard to trust or prove long after it was made.
tldr.mechanism: CAdES extends CMS signed data with extra signed and unsigned attributes. A basic signature can be built up with trusted time-stamps, references to or copies of certificates and revocation data, and finally archive time-stamps, forming a ladder of formats from CAdES-BES to CAdES-A.
tldr.outcome: The result is evidence usable in a later dispute. The RFC is Informational, a transposition of ETSI TS 101 733 V.1.7.4 that is technically equivalent to it, and it obsoletes RFC 3126.

today: RFC 5126 is an Informational document that obsoletes RFC 3126, and no later RFC is recorded as replacing it. Its contents are a transposition of ETSI TS 101 733 V.1.7.4 and are technically equivalent to it, and the technical contents are maintained by ETSI.

sections.title: Introduction and Scope
sections.content:
The document covers electronic signatures for transactions of many kinds, including business transactions such as purchase requisitions, contracts and invoices, where long-term validity matters and where there must be evidence of validity even if the signer or the verifying party later tries to deny, that is repudiate, the validity of the signature. It can be used for a transaction between an individual and a company, between two companies, or between an individual and a governmental body. The document is independent of any environment and can be applied to smart cards, GSM SIM cards, or special programs for electronic signatures.

The scope covers electronic signature formats only; the aspects of electronic signature policies are defined in RFC 3125 and in an ETSI technical report. The document defines a number of formats, including signatures that can remain valid over long periods, and specifies the use of Trusted Service Providers, such as Time-Stamping Authorities, and the data that needs to be archived, such as cross-certificates and revocation lists, so that the requirements of long-term signatures can be met.

The base is public key cryptography producing digital signatures supported by public key certificates, together with time-stamping and time-marking services to prove the validity of a signature long after the normal lifetime of its critical elements has passed, and, as an option, ways to give very long-term protection against key compromise or weakened algorithms. The document builds on RFC 3852, the Cryptographic Message Syntax, on the X.509 framework, on RFC 3280, the Internet X.509 Public Key Infrastructure certificate and certificate revocation list profile, and on RFC 3161, the Internet X.509 time-stamp protocol. The formats are described in ASN.1, encoded using X.690, and are based on CMS, which is why they are called CAdES, for CMS Advanced Electronic Signatures. Another document, ETSI TS 101 903, describes the equivalent formats for XML signatures.
sections.plainLanguage: The document says what it is for: signatures that will still be worth something in a court or an audit years after they were made. It does not define a new cryptography; it adds evidence to signatures that already exist.

sections.title: The Parties: Signer, Verifier, Trusted Services and Arbitrator
sections.content:
The major parties in a transaction supported by these signatures are the signer, the verifier, the Trusted Service Providers and the arbitrator. The signer is the entity that creates the electronic signature, and when the signer digitally signs over data using the prescribed format this represents a commitment on behalf of the signing entity to the data being signed. The verifier is the entity that validates the electronic signature, which may be a single entity or multiple entities. Trusted Service Providers help to build trust relationships between the signer and the verifier, supporting them with services such as user certificates, cross-certificates, time-stamp tokens, CRLs, ARLs and OCSP responses. The arbitrator arbitrates in disputes between a signer and a verifier.

The document lists the kinds of trusted service provider it uses. Certification Authorities provide users with public key certificates and a revocation service. Registration Authorities allow the identification and registration of entities before a CA generates certificates. Repository Authorities publish CRLs issued by CAs, signature policies issued by Signature Policy Issuers, and optionally public key certificates. Time-Stamping Authorities attest that some data was formed before a given trusted time, while Time-Marking Authorities record that some data was formed before a given trusted time. Signature Policy Issuers define the signature policies to be used by signers and verifiers. In some cases Attribute Authorities are needed as well, providing users with attributes linked to public key certificates.

The document also introduces signature policies, which establish technical consistency when validating signatures. When a comprehensive policy is either explicitly indicated by the signer or implied by the data being signed, a consistent result can be obtained. When the policy is neither indicated nor derivable, or is incomplete, verifiers including arbitrators may obtain different results, so comprehensive signature policies are recommended from both the signer's and the verifier's point of view.
sections.plainLanguage: Two people matter most: the one who signs and the one who checks. Between them sit trusted services that hand out certificates, say when a certificate was revoked, and record the time. If the two sides later disagree, an arbitrator settles it.

sections.title: The Basic Signature Formats
sections.content:
The document defines a number of electronic signature formats that build on CMS by adding signed and unsigned attributes. Two basic forms are specified, the CAdES Basic Electronic Signature and the CAdES Explicit Policy-based Electronic Signature, and conformance to the document mandates that the signer create one of them.

A CAdES-BES contains the signed user data, for example the signer's document, as defined in CMS; a collection of mandatory signed attributes defined in CMS and in the Enhanced Security Services specification; additional mandatory signed attributes defined in the document itself; and the digital signature value computed on the user data and, when present, on the signed attributes. It may also contain a collection of additional signed attributes and a collection of optional unsigned attributes.

The mandatory signed attributes include content-type, which specifies the type of the encapsulated content being signed, and message-digest. The identification of the signer's certificate used to create the signature is always signed, through the signing-certificate attribute or the signing-certificate-v2 attribute. The second of the two forms, CAdES-EPES, adds a signature-policy-identifier attribute that must always be present, which states the policy the signature was made under. The document notes that RFC 3126, which this one replaces, used a different signing-certificate attribute, whose use is now deprecated because the structure of the signing-certificate-v2 attribute is simpler.
sections.plainLanguage: The plainest form of a CAdES signature is a document, a set of attributes that say what the document is and who signed it, and the signature value itself. The second form adds one attribute naming the rules the signer followed.

sections.title: The Ladder of Formats: T, C, X and A
sections.content:
Validating an electronic signature needs extra data, called validation data: public key certificates, revocation status information for each of them, trusted time-stamps applied to the digital signature, or otherwise a time-mark in an audit log, and where appropriate the details of the signature policy to be used. The validation data may be collected by the signer, the verifier, or both.

CAdES-T is a signature with trusted time associated with it, provided either as a time-stamp attribute added to the signature or as a time-mark kept by a trusted service provider. The time-stamp attribute holds a time-stamp token over the electronic signature value, and trusted time provides the first step towards long-term validity. CAdES-C adds to the CAdES-T the complete-certificate-references and complete-revocation-references attributes: the first holds references to all the certificates in the certification path used to verify the signature, and the second holds references to the CRLs and OCSP responses used. Storing references rather than values allows the certification path and the revocation information to live elsewhere, which reduces the size of a stored signature.

The extended forms go further. CAdES-X Long adds the certificate-values and revocation-values attributes, that is, the whole certificate path and the CRLs and OCSP responses themselves, which provides a known repository of the material needed to validate a CAdES-C and prevents that material from getting lost. CAdES-X Type 1 adds a time-stamp token over the CAdES-C itself, and CAdES-X Type 2 adds a token over the certification path and revocation information references; both protect the certificates, CRLs and OCSP responses in case of a later compromise of a CA key, a CRL key or an OCSP issuer key. CAdES-A, the archival form, builds on a CAdES-X Long, or a CAdES-X Long Type 1 or 2, by adding one or more archive time-stamps, and successive time-stamps protect the whole material against vulnerable hashing algorithms or the breaking of the cryptographic material or algorithms.
sections.plainLanguage: Each format in the ladder adds one more piece of evidence: a time, then references to the certificates, then the certificates themselves, then time-stamps over those, and finally archive time-stamps. The more you add, the longer the signature can be defended.

sections.title: Validation and Arbitration
sections.content:
The validation process produces one of three output statuses: invalid, incomplete validation, or valid. An invalid response indicates that either the signature format is incorrect or that the digital signature value fails verification, for example because the integrity check fails or because one of the certificates the verification depends on is known to be invalid or revoked. An incomplete validation response indicates that the signature validation status is currently unknown; additional information may become available later, allowing the electronic signature to be checked again. An incomplete validation may be because all the required certificates are not available or because the grace period is not complete. A valid response indicates that the signature has passed verification and complies with the signature validation policy.

Validation data includes CA certificates and revocation status information in the form of CRLs or certificate status information provided by an online service, and evidence that the signature was created before a particular point in time, which may be a time-stamp token or a time-mark. The document explains a grace period, which permits certificate revocation information to propagate through the revocation processes, from the time an authorized entity requests revocation to the time the information is available for the relying party; verifiers should wait until the end of the grace period to be sure the certificate was not revoked when the signature was time-stamped or time-marked.

A CAdES-C may be used for arbitration in a dispute between the signer and the verifier, provided that the arbitrator knows where to retrieve the signer's certificate, the cross-certificates and the required CRLs, ACRLs or OCSP responses referenced in the CAdES-C; that, when time-stamping is used, the certificate from the authority that issued the time-stamp token is still within its validity period and was not revoked at the time of arbitration; that, when time-marking is used, a reliable audit trail is available; that none of the private keys used to verify the signature chain has ever been compromised; that the cryptography used when the CAdES-C was built has not been broken; and that, if the signature policy can be identified, the arbitrator can determine the rules for validating the signature.
sections.plainLanguage: Checking a signature can end in three ways: it is wrong, it is right, or the checker does not yet have enough information. The third case is normal while revocation information is still spreading, which is why the document defines a waiting period.

sections.title: Conformance Requirements
sections.content:
For implementations supporting signature generation, the document defines conformance requirements for two forms of basic electronic signature, one of which must be implemented; the same is true for implementations supporting signature verification. The document only defines conformance requirements up to a signature with complete validation data, CAdES-C, so none of the extended and archive forms need to be implemented to conform. On verification, the inclusion of optional signed and unsigned attributes must be supported only to the extent that the signature is verifiable, and the semantics of optional attributes may be unsupported unless a signature policy says otherwise.

A system supporting CAdES-BES signers must, at a minimum, support generation of an electronic signature consisting of the general CMS syntax and content type, CMS SignedData with the version set to 3 and at least one SignerInfo present, the content-type and message-digest attributes, and one of the signing-certificate or signing-certificate-v2 attributes. A system supporting policy-based signers must support the same components plus the signature-policy-identifier attribute, which must always be present. A verifier with time-stamping facilities must support verification of the mandated components, the signature-time-stamp attribute, the complete-certificate-references and complete-revocation-references attributes, public key certificates, and either certificate revocation lists or the Online Certificate Status Protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: An implementation has to produce and check the basic formats, and it has to be able to handle time-stamps and revocation information. The long-lived archival formats are optional.

viz.caption: EACH CAdES FORMAT ADDS TO THE ONE BEFORE IT

layers.label: CAdES-A
layers.detail: Adds one or more archive time-stamps over the whole material

layers.label: CAdES-X
layers.detail: Adds time-stamps over the references, or the certificate and revocation values

layers.label: CAdES-C
layers.detail: Adds complete certificate and revocation references

layers.label: CAdES-T
layers.detail: Adds a trusted time over the signature value

layers.label: CAdES-BES or CAdES-EPES
layers.detail: The signed document, the signed attributes and the signature value

viz.caption: WHO IS INVOLVED IN A SIGNED TRANSACTION

items.title: Signer
items.text: Creates the electronic signature. Signing the data is a commitment on behalf of the signing entity.

items.title: Verifier
items.text: Validates the electronic signature, and may be one entity or several.

items.title: Certification Authority
items.text: Provides users with public key certificates and a revocation service.

items.title: Time-Stamping Authority
items.text: Attests that some data was formed before a given trusted time.

items.title: Time-Marking Authority
items.text: Records that some data was formed before a given trusted time.

items.title: Repository Authority
items.text: Publishes CRLs, signature policies and optionally public key certificates.

items.title: Signature Policy Issuer
items.text: Defines the signature policies to be used by signers and verifiers.

items.title: Arbitrator
items.text: Arbitrates in disputes between a signer and a verifier.

viz.caption: THE FORMS AND WHAT EACH ONE ADDS

cells: CAdES-BES
The signed document, the mandatory signed attributes and the signature value
The baseline a signer must produce
CAdES-EPES
A signature-policy-identifier attribute
A signature made under a stated policy
CAdES-T
A signature-time-stamp attribute, or a time-mark
Proves the signature existed before a trusted time
CAdES-C
Complete certificate and revocation references
Lets a verifier rebuild the certification path later
CAdES-X Long
The certificate and revocation values themselves
Keeps a known repository of what the references point at
CAdES-X Type 1 or 2
A time-stamp over the CAdES-C or over the references
Protects the references against a later compromise
CAdES-A
One or more archive time-stamps
Protects long-term signatures against weak hashing or broken algorithms
